Respiratory Illness Outbreak Disrupts Oil & Gas Services Work in Guernsey

A respiratory illness outbreak has hit the Oil & Gas Services & Equipment industry in Guernsey, forcing several firms to scale back operations and temporarily close affected sites as they work to contain the spread among employees.

According to the Guernsey Oilfield Workers’ Union, more than 60 staff across four major service providers have been confirmed ill since last week, with symptoms ranging from severe cough to fever and shortness of breath. The affected companies, including Channel Rig Solutions and Sable Engineering Services, have suspended maintenance and inspection work at two onshore facilities and one offshore support site as a precaution. 

Industry officials say containment measures are being enforced in line with health authority guidance. “We are prioritizing the well-being of our workforce and have implemented strict isolation protocols for affected personnel,” said Anna Le Page, health and safety director at Sable Engineering Services. “Essential operations are being maintained by skeleton crews where possible, but several non-critical projects are on hold.”

The outbreak has led to a staffing shortfall estimated at 18% across the impacted firms, according to the Guernsey Oil & Gas Services Association. Some facilities have reduced shift numbers, and others are operating at limited capacity to ensure distancing and minimize further infections.

Analysts warn that the longer-term impact on oilfield services schedules in Guernsey could be significant if the outbreak is not swiftly contained. “We’re already seeing delays in routine equipment servicing and site upgrades,” said industry consultant Tom Martel. “Prolonged disruption could affect contract timelines and future project planning.”

Union representatives are calling for additional protective equipment and more regular health screenings for all workers. “Our members’ safety must come first,” said union spokesperson Claire Gavet. “We urge all companies to act decisively until the outbreak is fully under control.”

The situation remains fluid, with health authorities monitoring developments and industry leaders meeting daily to coordinate responses.
